title: A deep time perspective on a rare anatomical variant: Torus mandibularis presence in Australopithecus africanus from Sterkfontein, South Africa
abstract: Abstract Mandibular tori are benign bony exostoses located on the lingual aspect of the mandibular corpus that are common in modern human populations but rarely reported in the hominin fossil record. Their aetiology remains unclear, with both genetic and environmental factors proposed, including masticatory stress and parafunctional activity. Here we describe a pronounced bilateral mandibular torus in Sts 52b, a subadult australopith specimen from Member 4 deposits at Sterkfontein, South Africa (ca. 2.8–2.1 Ma). The torus forms a large lingual projection extending from the canine-premolar region posteriorly along the mandibular corpus and is most consistent with a grade 4 expression. Morphologically, it is stemless, monocystic, and composed primarily of compact cortical bone, closely resembling common clinical presentations in modern humans. Its occurrence in a subadult is notable, as toral development is frequently attributed to cumulative masticatory loading and is typically reported in adults. Moreover, the rarity of mandibular tori among fossil hominins with robust masticatory adaptations suggests that elevated occlusal forces alone are insufficient to explain their development. Sts 52b represents one of the earliest and most pronounced examples of mandibular torus expression in the hominin fossil record, extending the known antiquity of this trait to beyond 2 million years.
